question: What actually is leaky gut in dogs?
answer: The lining of your dog's gut is one cell thick. That single layer absorbs everything he needs while blocking what he doesn't — toxins, bacteria, undigested food. Those cells are held together by tight junctions, regulated by a protein called zonulin. When inflammation makes the cells swell, those junctions break and holes open in a barrier meant to be sealed. Large undigested proteins and environmental chemicals then pass into the bloodstream, where the immune system treats them as invaders. That's leaky gut: not a disease in itself, but a broken border with consequences all over the body.

question: Why does my dog seem allergic to everything?
answer: Because the food is arriving somewhere it was never meant to be. When the gut barrier leaks, large undigested proteins enter the bloodstream directly. The immune system logs them as invaders and mounts a histamine attack the next time it meets them — so your dog develops reactions to protein after protein. This is why elimination diets can chase chicken, then beef, then lamb, then novel proteins, and never resolve anything. You're not finding the culprit food; you're watching a broken barrier generate new sensitivities. Fix the barrier and the list usually stops growing.

question: What is zonulin and why does it matter?
answer: Zonulin is the protein that regulates the tight junctions holding your dog's gut lining together. When zonulin behaves, the seal is impermeable. When it rises, the gaps between cells widen and things get through that shouldn't. It matters twice over: it's the mechanism behind leaky gut, and it's also how the problem gets measured — lab tests can assess zonulin levels as a marker of intestinal permeability. Anti-gliadin antibodies are the other marker sometimes used. Neither test is required to start fixing it; the diet work is identical either way.

question: What breaks the gut barrier in dogs?
answer: Five things, roughly ordered by how much an owner controls. Highly processed kibble — high starch feeds the wrong organisms and gives the lining nothing to rebuild with. Glyphosate — it behaves like an antibiotic and directly disrupts tight junctions, usually arriving via non-GMO crops sprayed at harvest to dry them: oats, peas, chickpeas, lentils. Surplus omega-6 and inflammatory fats, which keep the inflammatory machinery running with nothing to fight. Chronic stress, including yours — dogs read it and it lands in their gut. And medications: antibiotics, NSAIDs, steroids and acid reducers all damage either the lining or the flora that maintain it.

question: Can antibiotics cause leaky gut in my dog?
answer: They're one of the main causes — sometimes called the carpet-bombing effect, because they don't distinguish between the bacteria causing a problem and the ones maintaining the barrier. NSAIDs, steroids and acid reducers do damage too, by different routes. None of this means refuse necessary medication. It means each course has a cost worth planning to repair afterwards rather than discovering six months later when your dog is itchy and nobody can work out why. If your dog had antibiotics recently and skin or gut problems started after, that sequence is not a coincidence.

question: My dog has itchy skin and ear infections — could that be a gut problem?
answer: Very likely. Yeast is a gut problem wearing a skin costume. An imbalanced microbiome lets yeast flourish and push through the skin, showing up as itching, hot spots, recurring ear infections, a corn-chip smell, sticky ears and thickened skin. Treating the skin while the gut stays broken is exactly why it keeps coming back — you're managing the outlet while the source runs. Ears, armpits and paws are all fed by the same thing in the digestive tract, which is why fixing the gut clears all of them at once rather than one at a time.

question: What is ADR in dogs?
answer: "Ain't Doing Right" — the informal term vets genuinely use for a dog who's clearly off but won't localise to any specific diagnosis. Vague lethargy, not quite himself, nothing on the exam. It's one of the most common presentations of a gut barrier problem, because systemic low-grade inflammation makes a dog feel unwell everywhere and nowhere. If your dog has been ADR for a while with clean bloodwork, the gut is worth looking at before the next round of tests.

question: Can leaky gut cause behaviour problems in dogs?
answer: It's on the list, and the mechanism is real rather than hand-waving. The gut-brain axis is a genuine signalling pathway — the microbiome influences emotional state via the vagus nerve. Anxiety, reactivity and aggression all appear in dogs with chronic gut inflammation. Part of it is signalling and part is simpler: a dog in constant low-grade discomfort is not the same dog. If behaviour changed around the same time as skin or digestive problems started, treat those as one story rather than two.

question: How do I heal my dog's leaky gut, and in what order?
answer: Four phases, and the order matters more than the products. One: species-appropriate diet — low-starch, fresh, whole food, with glyphosate-sprayed legumes and grains out. This does most of the work, and skipping to supplements without it is why protocols stall around week three. Two: bone broth and colostrum — collagen and amino acids that help seal the junctions, plus immune support. These are foods, so they're early and cheap. Three: targeted repair with L-glutamine and zinc carnosine, which matters most after the assault has stopped rather than during it. Four: soothing botanicals as short-term cover while the repair happens underneath.

question: What does L-glutamine do for a dog's gut?
answer: It's the preferred fuel of the cells that line the gut — literally what they rebuild themselves with. That makes it a structural repair material rather than a symptom treatment, which is why it belongs in phase three of a protocol and not phase one. Giving L-glutamine while the diet is still feeding the problem is like laying bricks during an earthquake. Pair it with zinc carnosine, which helps restore the lining, and use both once the assault has actually stopped.

question: Does bone broth actually help a dog's gut, or is it hype?
answer: It genuinely helps, and the mechanism is straightforward: it's rich in collagen and amino acids, the raw materials the intestinal lining is rebuilt from. It helps seal the tight junctions rather than just soothing symptoms. It also has the advantage of being food rather than a supplement — cheap, easy to feed, hard to overdo. Colostrum works alongside it, supporting tissue repair and immune balance. Both belong early in a protocol for exactly that reason.

question: What supplements help leaky gut, and what does each one do?
answer: Sort them by job rather than by brand. Rebuilding the lining: bone broth, L-glutamine and NAG — structural repair. Inflammation: turmeric, ginger and quercetin, to quell the systemic immune fire so the barrier gets a chance to close. Microbiome: S. boulardii and soil-based probiotics, which displace pathogens without over-colonising — and S. boulardii being a yeast means it survives a course of antibiotics that would wipe out bacterial probiotics. Detox support: humic and fulvic acid plus milk thistle, protecting against glyphosate and supporting the liver that processes whatever the gut lets through.

question: Why is glyphosate a problem for my dog's gut specifically?
answer: Two reasons. It behaves like an antibiotic in the body, damaging the microbiome, and it directly disrupts the tight junctions holding the gut lining together — so it attacks the barrier from both sides at once. The route in is usually food: non-GMO crops sprayed at harvest to dry them, which means oats, peas, chickpeas and lentils. That's why grain-free foods, which lean heavily on legumes, are often more exposed than the grain-containing ones people switched away from. Humic and fulvic acid are used as a systemic protector against it.

question: How long does it take to heal leaky gut in a dog?
answer: Weeks to months, not days. You're rebuilding a physical structure out of raw materials, and that takes as long as it takes. Most people stop around week three, decide it didn't work, and go back to managing symptoms — the single most common reason these protocols fail. Improvement usually shows in stool first, then energy, then skin and coat last, because the coat reflects what was happening weeks ago rather than today. If you want to see the progress, write it down; you cannot hold six weeks of gradual change in your head.

question: Should I keep a health journal for my dog?
answer: Yes, and it's the most underrated thing on any protocol. Date, food, stool, itching, energy, ear smell. Subtle changes are the whole game with gut healing, and without a written baseline every check-in becomes a fresh worry instead of a comparison. It also enforces the discipline that makes protocols work: change one thing at a time. A protein change and a new supplement in the same week means neither result tells you anything, and you'll spend the next month guessing which to blame.

question: When should I stop treating my dog's gut at home and see a vet?
answer: Most of a gut protocol is genuinely home territory — diet, broth, probiotics, patience. But some things aren't. Blood in the stool, sustained weight loss, a dog going genuinely off his food, or vomiting that doesn't settle all need a vet rather than a longer supplement list. Same for a dog who's deteriorating rather than plateauing. The point of knowing the escalation line is that it lets you be confident everywhere else — you're not gambling, you're working inside a boundary you decided in advance.

question: Does stress really affect my dog's gut?
answer: Yes, and the pathway is physical rather than metaphorical. Fight-or-flight halts digestion and promotes gut inflammation and permeability — it's one of the recognised contributors to a leaky barrier. The part people don't expect: it includes your stress, not just his. Dogs read their owner's state closely and it lands in their gut. So a household in upheaval, a move, a new baby, or a stretch where you're worried and short-tempered is a genuine variable in a gut protocol, and worth noting in the journal alongside the food.

question: Can leaky gut cause joint pain or thyroid problems in dogs?
answer: Both appear in the symptom spectrum, because systemic inflammation doesn't respect organ boundaries. Once undigested proteins and chemicals are entering the bloodstream and the immune system is chronically activated, the effects show up wherever that particular dog is most vulnerable — joints, thyroid, skin, brain. It's why leaky gut presents so inconsistently between dogs, and why a dog with aching joints, a dull coat and some anxiety can have one cause rather than three.

question: My dog only has gas and loose stool. Is that leaky gut?
answer: It might be, but the digestive symptoms are actually the minority presentation. Gas, bloating, reflux and chronic loose stool are what people expect from a gut problem — and plenty of leaky gut dogs never show them prominently, presenting instead as skin, ears, joints or behaviour. So the absence of dramatic digestive signs doesn't rule it out, and their presence doesn't confirm it. Look at the whole picture: recurring ear infections plus itchy paws plus soft stool plus a dog who seems off is a far more convincing pattern than any single symptom.

question: Why do soothing herbs like slippery elm need to be short-term?
answer: Because they work by coating rather than repairing. Mucilaginous herbs form a protective jelly-like layer over irritated tissue, lowering inflammation and letting healing happen underneath — genuinely useful as short-term cover in phase four of a protocol. But they also interfere with absorption of other nutrients and medications, and more importantly a dog who NEEDS them daily to hold a normal stool is telling you something. That's a masked problem, not a supplement requirement, and it's a signal to look for a hidden pathogen or overgrowth rather than keep bandaging.
